leads.name: Camberley Sequoiadendron Avenue
leads.reason: An avenue, not a single collectible point: originally 218 trees, now roughly 113 giant sequoias (Sequoiadendron giganteum) planted 1865 by Frederick Street as a memorial to the Duke of Wellington (who lived nearby at Stratfield Saye), running about 1.1km along the B3348 through Camberley/Heatherside. Fails the avenue/whole-wood exclusion in BRIEF_RESEARCH.md hard limits: no single obvious place to stand. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellingtonia_Avenue, glendale-services.co.uk. Distinct from the single named 'Wellington's Wellingtonia' specimen tree at Stratfield Saye itself, which is verified separately.

leads.name: Yews of Kingley Vale
leads.species_basis: genus read from the tree's own name; ask the reader which species
leads.reason: A whole wood, not a single collectible point. Kingley Vale is a c.120-hectare National Nature Reserve near Chichester containing one of the finest yew woods in Europe, spread across a valley; a 2012 dedicated survey (Peter Norton, ancient-yew.org) catalogues 51 of its oldest yews individually, with ages estimated at 500 to perhaps 2,000 years (the upper figure considered unlikely by the survey itself) and girths over 5m for the oldest. No single named specimen with one obvious place to stand was found in this pass (no 'King of Kingley Vale' or equivalent single-tree name turned up); the attached photos are generic views of the grove/forest rather than one identifiable tree. Fails the avenue/whole-wood exclusion the same way an avenue does: there is no one spot to send a visitor to. Unlike the Borrowdale Yews (published, bwd_001), which are a compact 'Fraternal Four' at a single viewpoint made famous by name via Wordsworth's poem, Kingley Vale is a dispersed reserve. If a future pass finds one specifically named, individually famous yew within it (the survey PDF lists 51 by number/description and could be mined for one), that could be a fresh lead; not established in this pass.

leads.name: Nocton Hall Chestnut
leads.species_basis: genus read from the tree's own name; ask the reader which species
leads.reason: Access fails hard rule 10. Nocton Hall (Lincolnshire) is a privately owned ruin (Leda Properties Ltd), on English Heritage's Buildings at Risk register, burnt out a second time in 2004 and left an unstable shell; the parish council/local sources describe the perimeter as fenced (North Kesteven District Council had to push the owner to secure it) and the grounds as overgrown, with 'the fine specimen trees hidden by more native species'. No source found describing any public right of way or open access to the grounds; this reads as private land under redevelopment, not somewhere a visitor can walk in without permission. Also flagging a dating problem even if access is ever resolved: local sources themselves note the tradition that Catherine Howard planted the tree in 1541 'seems rather unlikely' because horse chestnut was not introduced to Britain until the late 16th century, i.e. after her 1542 execution, a bridge claim the sources themselves question. Wikipedia states 'the tree still stands today' but this is undated and no post-2010 photo or report of it was found in this pass. Sources checked: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocton_Hall, nocton.blogspot.com, geograph.org.uk/photo/1731217, search results referencing English Heritage buildings-at-risk status.

leads.name: Wesley's tree
leads.reason: Dead and removed. This is the historic elm in Stony Stratford Market Square (Milton Keynes, Buckinghamshire, grid SP 786 403), under which John Wesley preached on 30 July 1777 and on other occasions. A 2007 geograph photo already shows 'the decaying remains of an ancient Elm'; further sources (mkheritage.org.uk local history pages) confirm it was ravaged by Dutch elm disease and damaged by two arson/vandalism fires, reduced to a charred hollow, and the remains have since been removed entirely. A young oak sapling has been planted on the site with a commemorative plaque, but it is a recent, unremarkable planting rather than the historic tree itself and has no age or dendrological interest of its own, so it does not pass as a living successor the way the Elm of Saint-Gervais precedent does. Never a collectible entry per the alive-now rule; could be mentioned as context in a future Stony Stratford/Milton Keynes story if a genuinely notable living tree is found there. Sources: geograph.org.uk/photo/569833, mkheritage.org.uk/archive/jt/tw/docs/4.html and mkheritage.org.uk/archive/mkm/stonystratford/docs/Tour/5marketsquare.html.

leads.name: Ormiston Yew
leads.species_basis: genus read from the tree's own name; ask the reader which species
leads.why: Verified 2026-09-06: alive, roughly 1,000 years old (Wikipedia's own history page gives a partial ring count of 750 years and a first written mention in 1474; scotlands-yew-trees.org gives a 592cm girth and says it 'could well be around a thousand years old'). John Knox reportedly preached under it in the 1540s. BLOCKED rather than shipped: the East Lothian Courier reports the tree was withdrawn from Scotland's Tree of the Year by its own landowner, who did not want attention drawn to it because of health problems more visitors seeking it out could worsen, and the Woodland Trust found the landowner's reasons compelling and complied. That is a deliberate decision by the people who know the tree not to encourage more visitors, the same category hard rule 10 protects even though scotlands-yew-trees.org itself still lists the site as public access. Do not resurrect this one without new evidence the health concern has passed.

leads.name: Wallace Yew
leads.species_basis: genus read from the tree's own name; ask the reader which species
leads.why: Verified and NOT shipped, 2026-08-29. Alive as of a 2021 photograph and behind a protective fence at Elderslie beside the Wallace monument, but wrecked: set on fire in 1978, and a storm on 12 January 2005 tore away the better-growing half and split the trunk almost to the ground. Age is genuinely disputed rather than merely unknown, 300 years by expert estimate against a 700-year tradition tying it to William Wallace himself, with 18th-century parish records already calling it ancient. Source: scotlands-yew-trees.org. Held on the walk-across-town test rather than on any rule; revisit if a recent photograph shows it worth the trip.

blocked.name: The Poem Tree
blocked.reason: Dead. The beech died in the 1990s, rotted while standing, and collapsed in July 2012; the decayed trunk disintegrated when a crane tried to make it safe. Remains left in situ as habitat, no replacement planted; a 1994 memorial stone nearby carries a 1965 rubbing of Joseph Tubb's carved poem. Confirmed via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Poem_Tree, 2026-09-06. Never a collectible entry per the alive-now rule; could be mentioned as context in a Wittenham Clumps story about a different living tree if one is ever found there.

blocked.name: Robin Hood's Larder
blocked.reason: Dead and gone, not merely dead-standing. Also known as the Butcher's Oak / Slaughter Tree / Shambles Oak, a hollow veteran (24 ft / 7.3 m circumference) in Sherwood Forest, badly burnt in the late 19th century and again in 1913, then fell in a gale in 1961; Wikipedia states no trace remains today. The only photos on file (1880, 1913) predate its fall by decades, which was exactly the red flag worth checking. Confirmed via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hood%27s_Larder, 2026-09-06. Not a collectible entry.
